source: TMUA 2019 · Paper 2 · Question 12 · Official worked answer

hints.title: Compare events before calculating
hints.body: If all three chosen students study Mathematics, the second student certainly does. Every outcome counted in T is therefore also counted in S.
hints.recap: An event contained in another event cannot have a greater probability.
hints.pitfall: There is no need to multiply three probabilities. The draws are not independent because the students are different.
hints.pause: Which must be smaller or equal: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>?

recall.reminder: An event contained in another event cannot have a greater probability.

hints.title: Compare the second and third events
hints.body: Ask whether every outcome in which the second student studies Mathematics also belongs to the event that at least one of the three does.
hints.recap: Containment of events gives an inequality between their probabilities.
hints.pitfall: The probability of an event concerns every outcome in that event.
hints.pause: Establish this containment and combine it with your first comparison.

recall.reminder: Containment of events gives an inequality between their probabilities.

hints.title: Decide whether the inequalities are strict
hints.body: For each containment, look for an outcome in the larger event but outside the smaller one. Use the intended setting with both Mathematics and non-Mathematics students.
hints.recap: Strict probability inequalities require possible extra outcomes.
hints.pitfall: If everyone studied Mathematics, the three probabilities would coincide.
hints.pause: Supply the distinguishing outcomes and then order the probabilities.

recall.reminder: Strict probability inequalities require possible extra outcomes.

solution:
1. Compare all three with the second student. Every selection in which all three students study Mathematics also has a Maths student second. Thus T≤S.

2. Compare the second student with at least one. If the second student studies Mathematics, at least one of the three does. Thus S≤R.

3. Establish strictness. Reading “most” as the intended mixture of Maths and non-Maths students, each larger event has additional possible outcomes: non-Maths first/Maths second gives S without T, while Maths first/non-Maths second gives R without S.

Therefore T<S<R: answer F. Exact class sizes and independence calculations are unnecessary.
